CORVID SYSTEMS — ON-CALL ESCALATION POLICY (v3, effective March)

1. Severity Definitions
SEV1: user-facing outage affecting more than 25% of traffic, any confirmed data loss, or any confirmed security breach. Page on-call immediately, no exceptions.
SEV2: user-facing degradation affecting 5-25% of traffic, sustained for more than 10 consecutive minutes. Page on-call immediately.
SEV3: degradation affecting less than 5% of traffic, or any internal-only tooling issue. Open a ticket; handle on the next business day. Do not page.

2. Exceptions
- Alerts firing during a published maintenance window are never paged, regardless of computed severity, unless a SEV1 condition is independently confirmed by a human.
- Alerts that auto-resolve within 3 minutes are not paged unless they recur 3 or more times within a 30-minute window.

3. Escalation chain: primary on-call -> secondary on-call (15 min no ack) -> engineering manager (30 min no ack) -> VP Engineering (60 min no ack). Secondary on-call should always check the #maintenance-calendar channel before acknowledging a page, since a large fraction of after-hours noise correlates with planned work. Every page, paged or suppressed, must still be logged in the incident tracker with a reason code so that the weekly on-call review has a full picture of alert volume.

4. Notes on judgment calls
These rules are meant to reduce needless pages, not to replace judgment. If an on-call engineer believes a SEV1 condition exists that the automated severity score is missing — for example, a slow-burning data corruption issue that would not show up as a traffic drop — they should page regardless of what this policy says, and note why in the incident log.

---

CASE LOG — Incident #7734
09:00 UTC — Scheduled maintenance window begins for search-index-cluster (published one week ago in #maintenance-calendar, window is 09:00-11:00 UTC). The maintenance is a planned index rebuild that is known to cause elevated error rates on that cluster while it re-shards.
09:22 UTC — Alert fires: search-index-cluster error rate at 18%, affecting an estimated 7% of total site traffic
09:26 UTC — Alert still firing; elapsed duration 4 minutes
09:31 UTC — Alert still firing; elapsed duration 9 minutes. On-call engineer Priya checks dashboards and confirms this matches the expected behavior during a planned index rebuild. No SEV1 condition (no outage over 25%, no data loss, no security issue) is present.
09:31 UTC — Priya adds a note to the ticket referencing the maintenance window and goes back to what she was doing.
10:58 UTC — Error rate on search-index-cluster drops back to baseline as the index rebuild finishes.
11:00 UTC — Maintenance window closes on schedule. Priya closes ticket #7734 with reason code 'expected-during-maintenance, no page required.'

state:
POSTMORTEM: Checkout Latency Incident — Sept 15
Status: Closed
Author: Priya Shah

Summary
On September 15, checkout page load times increased from a baseline of ~400ms to over 6 seconds for approximately 35 minutes, between 14:02 and 14:37 UTC. The incident was declared SEV2, paged to on-call, and resolved by rolling back a configuration change. No data was lost and no payments were double-charged. The incident was fully resolved and closed on September 15; this document was written up on September 17 for the team retro.

Timeline (Sept 15)
14:02 — Latency alert fires for checkout-service (p95 latency > 5s)
14:04 — On-call engineer Marcus paged, acknowledges within 2 minutes
14:09 — Marcus identifies a config deploy at 13:58 that raised the connection-pool timeout to an unusually high value
14:15 — Marcus begins rollback of the config change
14:22 — Rollback deployed to 50% of hosts, latency starting to improve on those hosts
14:31 — Rollback deployed to 100% of hosts
14:37 — Latency back to baseline (~410ms p95), incident marked resolved
14:40 — Customer support notified so they could close out the ~60 support tickets that had come in during the incident

Root Cause
A configuration change intended for a different service (search-index-cluster) was accidentally applied to checkout-service due to a shared config template. The change raised connection pool timeouts, causing connections to queue up under normal load.

Impact
- ~35 minutes of degraded checkout performance
- No full outage: checkout remained usable, just slow
- No data loss, no duplicate charges
- Approximately 60 customer support tickets related to slow checkout

Action Items
1. Split the shared config template so checkout-service and search-index-cluster can no longer accidentally share settings. Owner: Marcus. Status: DONE (merged Sept 16).
2. Add a pre-deploy diff review step that flags cross-service config changes. Owner: Priya. Status: IN PROGRESS, targeting end of month.
3. Send a short apology note to the ~60 affected support tickets. Owner: Support team. Status: DONE (sent Sept 15, same day).

This incident is closed. No further action is expected before the two remaining action items above are completed.

Contributing Factors
- The shared config template made it easy for a change meant for one service to silently apply to another.
- There was no automated diff review that would have caught a cross-service config change before deploy.
- On-call runbooks did not previously call out connection-pool timeout as a metric to check first for checkout latency, which cost Marcus a few minutes of initial investigation.

Lessons Learned
Shared infrastructure templates are convenient but risky when two services have very different traffic patterns. The team agreed in the retro that any future shared template needs an owner and a change-review requirement before it can be edited.

[Monitoring] 6 alerts fired within the same 60-second window at 04:02 UTC:
1. api-gateway-us: latency spike, transient network blip, auto-resolved after 45s
2. api-gateway-eu: latency spike, transient network blip, auto-resolved after 40s
3. cdn-edge-12: latency spike, transient network blip, auto-resolved after 50s
4. cache-cluster-3: latency spike, transient network blip, auto-resolved after 35s
5. orders-db replica-3: replication stopped at 04:02 UTC, still not caught up, NOT auto-resolving, manual intervention required
6. search-index-cluster: latency spike, transient network blip, auto-resolved after 55s
Root cause of items 1-4 and 6: a brief upstream network blip confirmed by the network team, all self-healed.

Incident channel #ops-alerts:
04:03 — Nina: lots of noise here, anyone see actual impact?
04:04 — Raj: network team already confirmed a brief blip on the east-coast backbone, that explains 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6
04:06 — Raj: #5 is different though, replication has been stopped since 04:02 and isn't recovering on its own, lag is now 8 minutes and climbing
04:07 — Nina: paging myself in for #5, the rest can stay auto-resolved
04:15 — Nina: confirmed replica-3 hit a disk I/O error partway through a write, which is what wedged replication. restarting the replication process manually now
04:24 — Nina: replication restarted cleanly, lag is draining, down to 3 minutes and falling
04:41 — Nina: lag fully caught up, replica-3 healthy again. keeping an eye on it for the next hour before I close this out, but no further action needed from anyone else
05:45 — Nina: closing #5, stayed healthy the whole hour. will file a ticket tomorrow to see if we can get disk I/O errors on replicas to auto-retry instead of wedging replication entirely, so this doesn't need a manual restart next time

Postmortem note, filed the next day: The five transient alerts (1-4, 6) were all traced to the same east-coast network blip and required no changes. The orders-db replica-3 issue was different in kind, not just severity: a disk controller on that specific host logged a transient I/O error mid-write, which caused the replication thread to hang rather than retry. Because our alert grouping dashboard displayed all six alerts in the same visual cluster with the same yellow color, it took Raj and Nina about four minutes to notice that #5 needed different handling. Action item: change the alerting dashboard so replication-specific alerts are visually distinct from generic latency alerts, so a real issue doesn't have to be spotted by someone reading each line individually during a noisy multi-alert window. Owner: Raj, target: end of next sprint. No customer-facing impact occurred; the orders-db read path stayed healthy throughout since only the replica, not the primary, was affected.
